{"self_assessment": "**Impact:** I sketched the fish on the scratch pad early and the table adopted it right away. Everyone took a stroke from it, so the build went up quickly. At the last check, a trace from the start showed all 98 dominoes connected, nose to both tail tips. I can't see the final fall, so I can't promise the judge reads it as a fish. The design is a plain outline: body, forked tail, nothing else. We had about 150 dominoes unused and never added an eye, fins or other cues that might have helped recognition. I chose the safe, readable option, and I'd weigh that trade-off more carefully next time.

**Execution:** I laid the start and the top line, then inspected the tail junction, the riskiest joint. I found and nudged one slightly off-line domino there. After that I kept hands off to avoid bumps, which the rules suggest is the main remaining risk. The cost is that I stopped improving the picture once it was connected, when I could have used the spare time and dominoes.

**Collaboration:** When Maya asked for the pad, I told her it already held the full fish and pointed her to the bottom line. That avoided duplicate sketching, and she, Tom and Leo each took a stroke without conflict. I asked people to keep clear of the tail joint, and they did. I could have been less repetitive with status updates, since I said the same thing to the manager several times.

**Leadership:** I set the plan, assigned strokes by name, and kept the table informed with short updates and a countdown near the end. The mood stayed calm and cheerful. I led mainly by coordinating, and I could have used the idle minutes to ask the team whether a few extra telltale features were worth adding."}
